anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statements or transaction scopes are written so inefficiently that they process more data, rows, or time than business requirements mandate.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Physical table, index, or partition structures are mis-aligned with access patterns, forcing even well-written queries onto sub-optimal access paths.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Old row versions and rollback information accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating storage and visibility-check cost.

When all three conditions coexist, the database exhibits compounded symptoms: end-user requests and background jobs show extreme and highly variable latencies; execution plans tilt toward full table or index scans that traverse bloated heaps and sparsely populated pages; slow-query logs are dominated by repetitive, wide-scan statements whose response times deteriorate steadily over the lifetime of the instance; buffer cache hit ratios fall despite rising memory pressure because enlarged tables consume more pages; DML operations stall during index maintenance and VACUUM/garbage-collection contention, and long-running transactions keep old snapshots alive, preventing space reclamation. Administrators may observe runaway table and index sizes, relentless autovacuum or purge activity that never catches up, escalating I/O utilisation, and application-level timeouts that are hard to attribute to a single layer.

Causally, inefficient SQL logic initiates excessive reads and writes, amplifying row churn and version creation. Because the underlying schema lacks selective or covering indexes, these statements must scan large portions of tables, touching many more rows than necessary and generating a high volume of MVCC undo or version records. The resulting bloat further degrades access paths, as query plans now operate on swollen data structures, worsening scan cost and skewing statistics. Simultaneously, the schema’s deficient indexing slows cleanup workers, which must traverse non-pruned partitions and wide indexes to locate obsolete versions. As long-running, chatty transactions from the flawed workload hold snapshots open, background cleaners cannot advance the version horizon, so space consumption and visibility-check overhead spiral upward. Each anomaly thus feeds the next: bad SQL intensifies data churn, poor physical design magnifies I/O and lock footprint, and overwhelmed MVCC maintenance inflates storage and latency, creating a self-reinforcing performance collapse in OLTP environments.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the amount of time with no network activity after which the operating system should send a TCP keepalive message to the client.
entry.trigger_condition: A TCP client connection has no network activity longer than tcp_keepalives_idle on systems supporting TCP_KEEPIDLE or an equivalent socket option.
entry.workload_impact: Starts TCP keepalive probing for an otherwise idle client connection; together with interval and count settings this can lead to dead connection detection.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
